items.zh: 四無量心 · 修捨證捨

zh: 第四、釋修捨證捨，亦為二：一者、正明修捨方法，如佛說：「若比丘以捨相應心，無瞋無恨，無怨無惱，廣大無量，善修。」捨相應心者，行者從喜定出，心自思念：「若慈與眾生樂，悲欲拔苦，喜令歡喜，而計我能利益，不忘二事，即非勝行。譬如慈父益子，不求恩德，乃曰真親。復次，眾生得樂有多因緣，不獨由我，若言我能與樂，則為過分。復次，慈心與樂，但是得解，然諸眾生實不得樂，若以為實，即是顛倒。復次，是諸眾生受苦樂，憂喜心生。憂喜心生即是結使，難得解脫。我今欲與清淨善法，不應住此三心。復次，我雖慈悲愛念，於彼無益，今當捨此三心，行諸善法，實利眾生。」
en: Fourth, explaining the cultivation and realization of equanimity: this too has two parts.

First, directly clarifying the method of cultivating equanimity, as the Buddha says: "There is a monk who, with a mind corresponding to equanimity, free of anger, free of resentment, free of enmity, free of vexation, vast and immeasurable, cultivates it well." As for the mind corresponding with equanimity: the practitioner, emerging from the concentration of sympathetic joy, reflects within: "If loving-kindness gives sentient beings happiness, compassion wishes to draw out their suffering, and sympathetic joy brings them delight, and yet I still reckon myself as able to benefit them, unable to forget these two matters, this is not yet the superior practice. It is like a loving father who benefits his own child without seeking any gratitude or reward in return — only this is called true parental affection. Furthermore: sentient beings attain happiness through many causes and conditions, not through myself alone; to say that I myself am able to give them happiness would be to overstate my own part in it. Furthermore: loving-kindness's giving of happiness is itself only a matter of understanding attained — sentient beings do not, in truth, actually attain happiness, and to take this as literally real would itself be a form of inverted thinking. Furthermore: these very sentient beings, undergoing suffering and happiness, give rise to worry and delight in turn — and this arising of worry and delight is itself nothing but a fetter, difficult to be liberated from. I now wish to give them the pure, wholesome dharma instead, and should not remain dwelling in these three states of mind. Furthermore: although I hold loving-kindness and compassion toward them, this brings them no true benefit in itself — I should now relinquish these three states of mind, and instead practice the various wholesome dharmas that truly benefit sentient beings."

zh: 如是念已，即捨三心，一心發願：「願一切眾生皆得妙捨莊嚴，令我悉見。」作是念已，即入禪定，用念清淨心取於親人受不苦不樂之相，一心緣之。若有異念，攝之令還，令於心想的的分明，見於前人受不苦不樂，如是次第緣中人、怨人、十方、五道一切眾生皆是不苦不樂，其心平等。是則略明修捨方法。二者、明捨定發相。行者如是修已，正念福德善根力故，作是緣時，三昧便發，即於定中不加功力，任運見於所愛親人受於不苦不樂之相，了了分明。於禪定中雖見眾生，心無憎愛，乃至十方、五道眾生亦復如是。行者爾時於此定中見諸眾生皆是捨相，三昧開發，無有動轉，深妙堅固，其心安隱，平等不二，是名捨相應心。無瞋無恨，無怨無惱，廣大無量，善修之義，並如上說。
en: Having reflected in this way, one relinquishes these three states of mind, and, with a single mind, makes this vow: "May all sentient beings attain this same subtle equanimity, adorned in its fullness — may I come to see this in every case." Having made this vow, one then enters dhyāna-concentration, using a mind of pure mindfulness to take up the mark of a loved one experiencing neither suffering nor happiness, fixing the mind single-mindedly upon this. Should some other thought arise, one gathers the mind back in, making the mental image entirely clear and distinct, seeing this person before one experiencing neither suffering nor happiness — extending this, in the same sequence, to a neutral person, an enemy, and, further still, to every sentient being throughout the ten directions and the five realms, all alike experiencing neither suffering nor happiness, the mind held perfectly equal throughout. This, in brief, describes the method for cultivating equanimity.

Second, clarifying the mark of the equanimity concentration's own arising. The practitioner, having cultivated in this way, through the power of right mindfulness, merit, and wholesome roots, taking up this object, samādhi is thereupon brought forth; within concentration, without any further application of effort, one sees, spontaneously and of its own accord, the mark of the loved one experiencing neither suffering nor happiness, entirely clear and distinct. Within this dhyāna-concentration, although sentient beings are seen, the mind holds neither aversion nor attachment toward them, and the same holds, further still, for sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the five realms. The practitioner, at this point, sees every sentient being alike bearing this same mark of equanimity within this concentration, samādhi opening and unfolding, utterly unmoved, deep, subtle, and secure, the mind at peace, equal throughout without any duality at all — this is named the mind corresponding with equanimity. Free of anger, free of resentment, free of enmity, free of vexation, vast and immeasurable, and the sense of "cultivated well" — all exactly as already described above.

zh: 問曰：前三種心中，應有福德，是捨心於眾生不苦不樂，有何等益？答曰：行者作是念：「一切眾生離苦得樂，失時即是苦，皆是惱累；得不苦不樂，則心安隱，始終無患。」以捨饒益故，得福亦大。復次，行者慈喜心時，或時愛著心生；行悲心時，或時憂悲心生。貪憂故，則功德尠薄。入是捨心，除此貪過，無諸煩惱，當知行捨福德甚大。復次，行者於捨心中能作種種益眾生事，是故福德增多。略說捨無量心竟。
en: Question: within the previous three states of mind, merit is bound to be present, but this equanimity, giving sentient beings neither suffering nor happiness, what benefit does it actually bring? Answer: the practitioner reflects: "When sentient beings pass from suffering into happiness, and then lose this happiness once more, this loss is itself a form of suffering — a trouble and a burden in every case. But attaining a state of neither suffering nor happiness, the mind remains at peace, free of affliction from beginning to end." Since equanimity thus truly benefits them, the merit gained through it is correspondingly great as well.

Furthermore: the practitioner, while practicing loving-kindness and sympathetic joy, may, at times, give rise to a mind of attachment; and, while practicing compassion, may, at times, give rise to a mind of grief and sorrow. Because of this craving and sorrow, the resulting merit is correspondingly thin and slight. Entering this state of equanimity, one removes this very fault of craving, free of every such affliction — one should know that the merit gained through practicing equanimity is exceedingly great. Furthermore: the practitioner, within this state of equanimity, is able to perform every kind of beneficial action toward sentient beings — hence the merit gained is increased all the more. This concludes, in brief, the immeasurable mind of equanimity.

zh: 問曰：悲喜捨中，何故不說法緣、無緣？答曰：義類前慈心可見，不煩重說。問曰：是四無量心，樂為二分，悲、喜、捨何故不作二分？答曰：樂是一切眾生所愛重，故作二分；苦不愛不欲，故不作二分。問曰：四無量發願入定見眾生，為實見，為心想見？答曰：見有二種：一、得天眼無量心，此實見。二者、但用得解憶想，緣眾生而入三昧。既證三昧，三昧力故，入則得見，出則不見。此為三昧得解之力，非實見。問曰：證四無量心，何故不分別支及體用、淺深、進退等相？答曰：證無量心時，亦非全無其義，但既無的文，故不須分別。
en: Question: within compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, why is loving-kindness's own distinction between taking dharma as its object and being objectless not spoken of again? Answer: the sense follows the same pattern already seen within loving-kindness, and may be readily understood — there is no need to repeat it here.

Question: among these four immeasurable minds, happiness is divided into two kinds, happiness and delight — why, then, are compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity not likewise each divided into two? Answer: happiness is what every sentient being cherishes and loves, and so it is divided into two; suffering is neither loved nor desired, and so it is not divided into two in the same way.

Question: when the four immeasurable minds make their vow and enter concentration to see sentient beings, is this a truly real seeing, or merely a seeing through mental imagination? Answer: seeing is of two kinds: one who has attained the immeasurable mind together with the heavenly eye sees truly and really; but one who merely uses understanding and mental recollection, taking sentient beings as an object in order to enter samādhi, upon actually realizing this samādhi, through the very power of the samādhi, sees them while within it, but no longer sees them once having emerged from it. This is the power of samādhi's understanding attained, not a truly real seeing.

Question: in realizing the four immeasurable minds, why are their factors, substance and function, depth, and progress and regression not distinguished, the way they were for the four dhyānas? Answer: at the moment the immeasurable minds are realized, it is not that this sense is entirely absent either — it is simply that, there being no definite text addressing it, it is not necessary to distinguish it here.

Equanimity's cultivation method is structurally distinct from the other three: rather than intensifying a positive wish toward beings, it is reached by critiquing the very presumption behind loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy — the quiet self-congratulation of "I am the one benefiting them" — and relinquishing it. The loving-father simile makes the point precisely: the parent who helps without seeking credit is "true" parental affection, implying the first three immeasurable minds, however genuine, still carry a residue of self-reference that equanimity alone removes. The closing defense of equanimity's merit gives three reasons rather than one: a state of neither suffering nor happiness leaves the mind at peace, free of the trouble of happiness gained and then lost; it removes the craving and sorrow that can creep into loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, and compassion; and, from within equanimity, the practitioner can still perform every kind of beneficial deed for sentient beings.

quiz.q: Reflecting that reckoning oneself a benefactor is not the superior practice, what simile does the practitioner use?
options: a loving father benefits his child seeking no reward; only this is true affection
a mother rejoicing at her child's recovery
quiz.why: Still reckoning oneself able to benefit beings is not the superior practice, like a loving father who benefits his child without seeking gratitude.

quiz.q: Why would saying "I can give beings happiness" overstate one's part?
options: beings attain happiness through many causes, not through me alone
happiness is contaminated and should not be given
quiz.why: Beings attain happiness through many causes and conditions, not through oneself alone, so claiming to give it is an overstatement.

quiz.q: Entering concentration to cultivate equanimity, what mark of the loved one is taken up?
quiz.why: One takes up the loved one experiencing neither suffering nor happiness. The other marks belong to loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy.

quiz.q: Equanimity gives beings neither suffering nor happiness. What benefit does it bring?
options: it makes beings reborn in heaven
happiness gained is suffering when lost; neither-suffering-nor-happiness leaves the mind at peace from beginning to end
it gives the practitioner supernormal powers
quiz.why: Passing into happiness and then losing it is itself suffering; neither suffering nor happiness leaves the mind at peace, so equanimity truly benefits beings.

quiz.q: What faults may arise while practicing loving-kindness, joy, and compassion, which equanimity removes?
options: attachment with loving-kindness and joy, grief with compassion; craving and sorrow thin the merit
quiz.why: Loving-kindness and joy may give rise to attachment, compassion to grief; equanimity removes this fault, so its merit is great.

quiz.q: Happiness is divided into two among the immeasurable minds. Why are the others not divided likewise?
options: happiness is cherished by all beings, so it is divided; suffering is not loved or desired, so it is not
they belong to the formless realm
quiz.why: Happiness is what all beings cherish, so it is divided into two; suffering is neither loved nor desired, so it is not.

quiz.q: When one sees beings in the immeasurable minds, is it real seeing or imagined seeing?
options: with the heavenly eye it is real; through understanding and recollection one sees within samādhi but not after, which is not real seeing
quiz.why: There are two kinds: with the heavenly eye the seeing is real; through understanding and recollection one sees within samādhi but not after emerging, which is the power of samādhi, not real seeing.

quiz.q: Why are factors, substance and function, depth, and progress not distinguished for the immeasurable minds?
options: the sense is not wholly absent, but there is no definite text, so it is unnecessary
quiz.why: The sense is not entirely absent, but since no definite text addresses it, there is no need to distinguish it.

quiz.q: Why are the dharma-object and objectless kinds not discussed for compassion, joy, and equanimity?
options: these belong to the formless realm
the sense follows loving-kindness and need not be repeated
quiz.why: The sense follows the same pattern as loving-kindness and may be readily understood, so it is not repeated.
